content: 1. Mathews M, Heath SL, Neufeld SM, Samaraseena A conducted an evaluation of physician return-for-service agreements in Newfoundland and Labrador, published in Healthcare Policy in 2013, which analyzed the effectiveness of these agreements in addressing physician shortages. 2. Devine SG, Williams G, Nielsen I explored the impact of rural allied health scholarships on workforce outcomes in rural and remote areas, as detailed in their 2013 study in Rural and Remote Health. 3. Renner DM, Westfall JM, Wilroy LA, and Ginde AA examined how loan repayment programs influence the recruitment and retention of rural healthcare providers in Colorado, as published in Rural and Remote Health in 2010. 4. Martineau T, Decker K, Bundred P discussed the phenomenon of brain drain among health professionals and proposed actionable solutions in their article in Health Policy. 5. Dieleman M, Cuong PV, Anh LV, and Martineau T identified factors influencing job motivation among rural health workers in northern Vietnam, as published in Human Resources for Health. 6. Iipinge SN, Hofnie K, van der Westhuizen L, and Pendukeni M conducted a case study in Namibia to understand health workers' perceptions of their working conditions. 7. Mangham LJ and Hanson K used a discrete choice experiment to investigate the employment preferences of public sector nurses in Malawi, as published in Tropical Medicine and International Health. 8. Martineau T, Lehmann U, Matwa P, Kathyola J, and Storey K analyzed factors affecting the retention of rural health workers in Malawi and South Africa, as reported by the World Health Organization in 2006. 9. Kotzee TJ and Couper ID explored interventions that South African doctors believe would help retain them in rural hospitals in Limpopo Province, as published in Rural and Remote Health in 2006. 10. Humphreys J, Wakerman J, Pashen D, and Buykx P reviewed retention strategies and incentives for health workers in rural and remote areas, identifying effective approaches. 11. Ashkenazi Y, Gordon M, and Rosen B described the use of financial incentives to attract medical residents to peripheral areas in Israel, as detailed in Health Policy. 12. Lisam S, Nandi S, Kanungo K, Verma P, Mishra J, and Mairembam D evaluated strategies for attracting and retaining health workers in remote areas of Chhattisgarh, India, as published in the Indian Journal of Public Health. 13. Solowiej K, Upton P, and Upton D developed a scheme to support the recruitment and retention of allied health professionals in rural areas, as detailed in the International Journal of Therapy and Rehabilitation. 14. Sirili N, Frumence G, Kiwara A, Mwangu M, Anaeli A, Nyamhanga T, et al. conducted a qualitative study on the retention of medical doctors at the district level in Tanzania, as published in BMC Health Services Research. 15. Goma FM, Tomblin Murphy G, MacKenzie A, Libetwa M, Nzala SH, Mbwili-Muleya C, et al. evaluated recruitment and retention strategies for health workers in rural Zambia, as reported in Human Resources for Health. 16. Reid S monitored the impact of a new rural allowance for health professionals, assessing its effectiveness in improving workforce retention. 17. Yong J, Scott A, Gravelle H, Sivey P, and McGrail M investigated the effects of rural incentive payments on the entry and exit of general practitioners, as published in Social Science and Medicine. 18. Singh D, Negin J, Otim M, Orach CG, and Cumming R examined the impact of payment and incentives on the motivation and focus of community health workers in lowand middle-income countries, as detailed in Human Resources for Health. 19. Janes R and Dowell A conducted a survey of rural general practitioners in New Zealand, capturing their perspectives on workforce challenges and solutions. 20. Mkoka DA, Mahiti GR, Kiwara A, Mwangu M, Goicolea I, and Hurtig A-K explored factors influencing working conditions for maternal healthcare providers in rural Tanzania, as published in Human Resources for Health. 21. Narayan V, John-Stewart G, Gage G, and O’Malley G highlighted the role of poor communication and job dissatisfaction in the attrition of rural health workers in Sierra Leone. 22. Codjia L, Jabot F, Dubois H, and the World Health Organization evaluated a program supporting the medicalization of rural health areas in Mali. 23. Zimmerman M, Shah S, Shakya R, Sundar Chansi B, Shah K, Munday D, et al. described a staff support program for rural hospitals in Nepal, as published in the Bulletin of the World Health Organization. 24. Belaid L, Dagenais C, Moham M, and Ridde V conducted a mixed-method study to understand factors affecting the attraction and retention of health professionals in rural Niger. 25. Darkwa EK, Newman MS, Kawkab M, and Chowdhury ME explored factors influencing the retention of doctors and nurses in rural healthcare facilities in Bangladesh. 26. Bilodeau H and Leduc N compiled an inventory of factors determining the attraction, installation, and retention of physicians in remote areas. 27. Glazebrook RM and Harrison SL identified obstacles and solutions for maintaining advanced procedural skills among rural and remote medical practitioners in Australia. 28. Manahan C and Lavoie JG reviewed international literature on factors influencing rural nurse retention. 29. Terry D, Lê Q, Nguyen U, and Hoang H studied workplace health and safety issues among community nurses and their impact on rural healthcare delivery. 30. Wurie HR, Samai M, and Witter S analyzed the retention of health workers in rural Sierra Leone through life history interviews. 31. The World Health Organization published a manual for primary healthcare workers on occupational health. 32. Franche RL, Murray EJ, Ostry A, Ratner PA, Wagner SL, and Harder HG examined work disability prevention among rural healthcare workers. 33. Lenthall S, Wakerman J, Opie T, Dollar M, Dunn S, Knight S, et al. investigated occupational stress among remote area nurses and proposed future actions. 34. George AS, McConville F, de Vries S, Nigenda G, Sarfraz S, and McIsaac M discussed violence against female health workers as a reflection of gender power imbalances. 35. The World Health Organization developed a framework for creating healthy workplaces, emphasizing the importance of supportive environments. 36. The International Labour Office and United Nations System Chief Executives Board for Coordination created a toolkit for mainstreaming employment and decent work. 37. Henderson LN and Tulloch J reviewed incentives for retaining and motivating health workers in Pacific and Asian countries. 38. Couper ID, Hugo JFM, Conradie H, Mfenyana K, and members of the CHEER collaboration analyzed factors influencing health professionals' decisions to practice in rural areas. 39. The Expanded Programme on Immunization developed training modules for mid-level managers, focusing on supportive supervision. 40. Rahman SM, Ali NA, Jennings L, Seraji MHR, Mannan I, Shah R, et al. identified factors affecting the recruitment and retention of community health workers in a newborn care intervention in Bangladesh. 41. Abbey M, Bartholomew LK, Nonvignon J, Chinbuah MA, Pappoe M, Gyapong M, et al. studied factors related to the retention of community health workers in a trial on community-based fever management in Ghana. 42. Watanabe M, Jennett P, and Watson M explored the impact of information technology on the physician workforce and healthcare delivery in isolated communities in Canada. 43. Gruen RL, Weeramanthri TS, Knight SSE, and Bailie RS reviewed the effectiveness of specialist outreach clinics in primary care and rural hospital settings. 44. Gagnon M-P, Duplantie J, Fortin J-P, and Landry R examined the effects of telehealth on medical human resource supply in remote regions. 45. Mbemba GIC, Bagayoko CO, Gagnon M-P, Hamelin-Brabant L, and Simonyan DA studied the influence of a telehealth project on healthcare professional recruitment and retention in Mali. 46. Komaromy M, Duhigg D, Metcalf A, Carlson C, Kalishman S, Hayes L, et al. introduced Project ECHO as a model for educating primary care providers about substance use disorder treatment. 47. Bagayoko C-O, Gagnon M-P, Traoré D, Anne A, Traoré AK, and Geissbuhler A shared lessons learned from the EQUi-ResHuS project in Mali, which used e-health to recruit and retain healthcare professionals in remote areas. 48. Bervell B and Al-Samarraie H conducted a comparative review of mobile health and electronic health utilization in sub-Saharan African countries. 49. Ly BA, Labonté R, Bourgeault IL, and Niang MN described the determinants of telemedicine use in Senegal, based on perceptions of physicians and project managers. 50. The Global Observatory for eHealth published a report on the potential of mobile technologies to transform healthcare delivery. 51. Masango S, Gathu K, and Sibandze S assessed the role of non-financial incentives in retaining Swaziland's health sector workforce. 52. Butterworth K, Hayes B, and Neupane B conducted a qualitative study on the retention of general practitioners in rural Nepal. 53. Connolly M, Sweet L, and Campbell D evaluated the impact of longitudinal rural medical student clerkships on clinical supervisors and hospitals. 54. Levesque M, Hatcher S, Savard D, Kamyap RV, Jean P, and Larouche C explored physician perceptions of recruitment and retention factors in areas with regional medical campuses. 55. Couper ID and Worley PS discussed the role of the journal Rural and Remote Health in addressing health and information challenges in Africa. 56. Wibulpolprasert S and Pengpaibon P reviewed Thailand's integrated strategies to address the inequitable distribution of doctors over four decades. 57. Gardiner M, Sexton R, Kearns H, and Marshall K evaluated the impact of support initiatives on retaining rural general practitioners. 58. Willis-Shattuck M, Bidwell P, Thomas S, Wyness L, Blaauw D, and Ditlopo P conducted a systematic review on the motivation and retention of health workers in developing countries. 59. The World Health Organization, World Bank, and USAID published a user guide on conducting discrete choice experiments for health workforce recruitment and retention in rural areas.
